schools.summary: Ellicott fixes the chronology on both sides — Isaac forty at his marriage, Abraham surviving it thirty-five years to see Esau and Jacob nearly grown.

Calvin reads the notice of age as the reason for the errand and grounds the ban on Canaanite marriage in the covenant separation rather than in Canaanite morals; Gill distinguishes Abraham's country from Canaan, which was his by promise only.
Henry gives the two motives for acting now and makes the two negatives — not a Canaanite, and not a journey for Isaac himself — a rule for parents.
Wesley states the same two cautions; Clarke adds the curse on Canaan as the older ground and reports the custom of proxy betrothal still keeping in the East.

debates.question: Why must Isaac not marry a Canaanite?

sides.position: because God had separated Abraham from them by covenant and appointed them to destruction
because Canaan already lay under the curse pronounced on him

themes: an old man setting his house in order
1.pericope_label: Abraham charges his servant to seek a wife from his own kindred

schools.summary: Gill calls the servant's question prudently asked; Calvin admires a man who will not swear rashly and notes he raises no doubt about Isaac.
Clarke explains from Calmet how strictly the ancients held themselves to the letter of an oath; Wesley and Henry take the angel as the ministry of guidance promised to the heirs.
Keil and Delitzsch ground the refusal in the call and the promise of the land; Ellicott weighs the two principles at stake and finds the ban on returning the weightier.
Henry draws the caution that oaths should be limited and understood before they are taken, not after.

outliers.note: Holds that intermarriage within the race was a means to an end and not a law for its own sake, while the ban on returning to Padan-aram was absolute.

themes: a servant who reads the oath first
5.pericope_label: The servant's scruple, and Abraham's answer

schools.summary: Ellicott argues from 'thigh' as the source of posterity that the gesture was a euphemism, making the oath one by the covenant of circumcision.
Clarke reaches the same conclusion through the Targums, paraphrases what the oath was understood to mean, and defends the rite against modern delicacy.

Calvin lays out the Jewish and Christian explanations, prefers the plainer, and declines to decide, insisting only that the rite was not profane since God's name was interposed; Gill reports the Targum's paraphrase.
Henry makes swearing an ordinance common to mankind, to be performed by whatever signs a country has appointed.

debates.question: What did putting the hand under the thigh signify?

sides.position: the covenant of circumcision, of which that member was the sign
holders: the Targums (as reported by Gill and Clarke)

sides.position: a token of a servant's subjection to his master
holders: some Jewish writers (as reported by Calvin)

sides.position: honour done to the blessed seed to come from Abraham's loins

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the size of the convoy, answers why Isaac did not go himself, and identifies Nahor's city as Haran; Keil and Delitzsch place it the same way.

Calvin reads the presents as the argument that would persuade a girl to leave home, and takes 'all the goods in his hand' as the narrative's own account of the servant's authority; Gill notes that kneeling is taught to camels, not natural.
Clarke reports the custom of giving rather than receiving a dowry, and the same practice of women drawing water still keeping in Bengal.
Henry makes the unnamed servant an example to all servants, and records the older reading of the errand as a figure of the church espoused by Christ's ministers.

debates.question: What does 'all the goods of his master were in his hand' mean?

sides.position: a schedule or inventory carried to show the family
holders: some Jewish interpreters (as reported by Calvin)

sides.position: the reason he could travel so splendidly — his master's whole substance was at his disposal

10.pericope_label: The journey to the city of Nahor, and the halt at the well

schools.summary: Gill notes he invokes not his own God but his master's; Calvin feels the difficulty of prescribing to God and resolves it by the secret impulse of the Spirit rather than by excusing the prayer.
Henry defends praying for particulars, admires the qualities the sign was designed to test, and notes where the man went to look for such a woman.
Clarke quotes Dodd's defence of asking a natural sign and then presses past it, holding that no use of the rational faculties could have decided this case.

debates.question: Was it lawful to ask for so specific a sign?

sides.position: yes — a prayer, not a limit set on God, and asking only what a good wife would naturally do
it departs from the modesty of prayer, and is excused only because the servant was moved by the Spirit

outliers.note: States the rule both ways: to expect a good end without the means is enthusiasm, and to expect good from the means without God's blessing is no better.

12.pericope_label: The servant's prayer at the well

schools.summary: Gill notes the prayer was mental and answered as the last words formed; Calvin observes that Rebekah had left home before it began, and makes the point about God ordering both movements rather than about speed.
Clarke marks how exactly providence fitted the circumstances; Wesley lists the qualities asked for and finds them all present.
Henry reads her conduct at the well as the whole argument — she minded her business and answered modestly.
Ellicott explains the flight of steps down to a spring-fed well and quotes a traveller's description of the same well outside Haran today.

outliers.note: Refuses to make the speed of this answer a rule, since delay is often expedient; what is proved is that the prayers of God's people are never in vain.

themes: the steps down to the well
15.pericope_label: Rebekah comes out to the well

schools.summary: Clarke makes her exceeding the request the proof that the kindness was her own, and rebukes the servant for letting her water ten camels unaided.
Gill lists everything the man wondered at, from her courtesy to the timing of her arrival; Calvin takes the wondering for real doubt and declines to excuse it away.
Ellicott reports that the rare verb is read by the ancient versions as gazing attentively in silence, so that the man is observing and concluding rather than merely astonished.

debates.question: What is the man doing while she waters the camels?

sides.position: wondering — astonished at how exactly his prayer was being answered
gazing attentively and holding his peace, in order to know
holders: the Septuagint, Syriac and Vulgate (as reported by Ellicott)

outliers.note: Says he cannot tell which to admire more, Rebekah's condescension or the servant's cold and apparently stupid indifference.

18.pericope_label: She waters the camels; the man watches

schools.summary: Ellicott shows from the later verse and from Ezekiel and Proverbs that the ornament was a nose-ring, and Keil and Delitzsch add that the man placed the ornaments on her in return for her kindness, not as a bridal gift.
Clarke rules out ear-rings from the singular number, follows Symmachus for the nose, and takes the second ornament for armlets rather than anklets.

Calvin reads the gift as an act of confidence and turns it into a warning against ornament, meeting the objection to a maiden accepting it from a stranger; Gill reconciles the order of gift and question with Schmidt.

debates.question: May Rebekah's jewels be pleaded in defence of ornament?

sides.position: no — particular examples do not license what the general law condemns, and those who cite her do not imitate her labour
they were customary betrothal gifts, no more disfiguring than ornaments worn today

22.pericope_label: The gold given, and her family named

schools.summary: Henry takes the thanksgiving clause by clause — praise for answered prayer, praise while the issue is still uncertain, praise for another's mercy, praise for being led.
Gill notes the words were spoken in Rebekah's hearing, so that she learned from them who he was and whence he came.

26.pericope_label: The servant bows and blesses the God of his master

schools.summary: Ellicott explains 'her mother's house' from the separate tent of a sheikh's wife, and traces Laban's standing as Rebekah's representative through the rest of the chapter.
Clarke allows the same domestic arrangement while thinking Bethuel probably dead; Wesley credits the welcome to Rebekah's report of the man's devotion.

Gill reads Laban's haste straight from the sight of the gold and calls his covetousness plain from the whole story; Calvin takes the simpler view that she went to her mother's chamber because she could tell it there more easily.
Henry says bluntly that here was a man there was something to be got by, and cites the proverb that a man's gift makes room for him.

debates.question: Why is the welcome so warm?

sides.position: Laban saw the gold and expected to be rewarded
hospitality was almost a matter of course in the East, though the gold may have sharpened it
they had heard of the man's worship and concluded he was blessed of God

outliers.note: Finds it remarkable that Laban should say 'blessed of Jehovah', since the family's monotheism was impure and their other gods were probably teraphim.

28.pericope_label: Laban runs out; the stranger is brought in

schools.summary: Henry makes the refusal to eat the measure of the man and reads the speech as advocacy, noting the tact of its opening and the objection it forestalls.
Clarke sets the gesture among eastern customs and hears an echo of it in the Lord's words about his own meat.
Gill takes the inventory of Abraham's wealth as spoken for the family's benefit rather than as boasting.
Keil and Delitzsch set out the speech as it stands, from the disclosure of identity to the charge repeated in its own words.

33.pericope_label: The errand told: Abraham's wealth and Abraham's charge

schools.summary: Henry sees in the retold exchange the care the servant took to leave the family free to consent or refuse.
Clarke notes the appeal to Abraham as the friend of God, and presses almah as meaning a pure virgin in the proper sense; he also dismisses the tale of a miraculous one-day journey.
Ellicott identifies almah as a young woman ripening for marriage, the word used of Miriam and of the mother of Immanuel.
Gill lets the repetition stand as the servant gave it, referring each clause back to the event.

sides.position: a young woman just ripening for marriage
a pure virgin in the proper sense, one still concealed from man

39.pericope_label: The servant retells Abraham's answer and his own prayer

schools.summary: Wesley says the man notes the prayer was mental to forestall the suspicion that Rebekah had overheard and obliged him; Clarke argues public prayer would have been out of place among servants with no stake in it.
Ellicott improves the idiom — before I had done speaking to my heart — and settles the ornament as worn on the nose.
Henry lingers on 'the right way' and reads the closing appeal as the fairness of a man who has dealt fairly.
Gill takes the final address as made to the whole family, and especially to Laban and Bethuel.

outliers.note: Calls fanciful the suggestion that turning to the right hand or the left hinted at seeking a wife among the descendants of Ishmael or Lot.

themes: tell me, and do not hold me in suspense
45.pericope_label: The retelling completed, and the question put

schools.summary: Calvin finds the submission of half-corrupted idolaters a rebuke to better-taught readers, and says Moses repeats the thanksgiving because neglect of it betrays shameful indolence; Gill weighs who actually spoke, given the singular verb.
Henry notes what they did not object, and identifies what they trusted — much to the servant's integrity, more to God's providence.
Wesley draws the plain conclusion about marriages that proceed from the Lord; Clarke takes Laban and Bethuel for brothers, the father being dead.
Ellicott keeps the father alive and explains the order by the estrangement polygamy produced; Keil and Delitzsch set out the order of thanks, gifts and food.

debates.question: Who is the Bethuel who answers with Laban?

sides.position: the father, old and leaving management to his son
a younger brother of that name, the father being dead
the father, placed after the brother because polygamy estranged fathers from their children

themes: the thing proceedeth from the LORD
glory to God, not to the angel
50.pericope_label: Laban and Bethuel consent; the servant worships

schools.summary: Gill describes the presents as proof of Abraham's wealth and of his liberality in furnishing his servant so amply.
Henry counts three motives at once — proof of his master's generosity, gratitude for the family's civility, and a means of ingratiating himself.
Keil and Delitzsch note the division between bride and relations; Ellicott explains that a wife had to be bought and that these were articles of substantial value, not ornaments merely.
Clarke distinguishes the earlier token of respect from this dowry, and traces the word behind 'precious things' through its other uses.

debates.question: Why do the gifts go to the brother and the mother, not the father?

sides.position: because Bethuel lay ill and died that very day
because polygamy had made the mother's tent the customary destination

schools.summary: Clarke marks that he ate only after the favourable answer, and canvasses every rendering of the disputed phrase for the delay; Wesley reads the request as reluctance after consent.
Henry praises a servant who preferred his work to his pleasure and reads the family's reluctance as proof that no pleasure in this world is unmixed.
Calvin sees the Lord impelling the man for Isaac's sake, and calls the year-or-months reading forced, hearing only a mother's tenderness; Gill notes Laban set before his mother as the chief speaker.
Ellicott prefers to take the decade as the name for a third of a month, which would make Terah's family reckon time in ten-day periods.

debates.question: How long a delay did the family ask for?

sides.position: about ten days
a year, or ten months
holders: Onkelos, Saadja and Rashi (as reported by Ellicott)

sides.position: a month of days
a decade, being a third of a month

54.pericope_label: The servant asks leave; the family ask for delay

schools.summary: Henry states the rule both ways: children ought not to marry without their parents' consent, nor parents marry them without their own.

Calvin guards the balance from the other side, holding parental authority sacred but denying the father any tyranny over an unwilling daughter; Gill supposes she had withdrawn out of modesty and had to be called.
Clarke takes her answer as deciding the whole business, and canvasses whether the question was about going at all or going at once.
Ellicott reads her readiness as of a piece with everything else shown of her, though she will never see her relatives again.

outliers.note: Defends her prompt answer against the charge of despising her father's house or being over-eager for a husband.

schools.summary: Gill insists the dismissal was affectionate and honourable; Calvin explains the office of a household nurse and the ancient custom of blessing a bride.
Clarke names the nurse Deborah and calls her going good sense and prudence, and sets the blessing among customs still kept; Wesley infers from the damsels that Rebekah drew water by choice.

Ellicott divides the blessing into fruitfulness and victory and notes the Hebrew has no word for a million; Keil and Delitzsch read the figure as hyperbole and match the second half to the promise after the binding of Isaac.
Henry thinks the family had heard of that promise and framed their blessing on it, and observes that nothing is said of a portion.

59.pericope_label: Rebekah is sent away with her nurse and the family's blessing

schools.summary: Ellicott places Lahai-roi in the Negeb, works out what the journey's length implies about Abraham's shifting stations, and prefers meditation to prayer for the rare verb; Keil and Delitzsch record Isaac's coming from that well.
Gill identifies the well as Hagar's and reports Onkelos and Jonathan for 'to pray'; Calvin explains Isaac's separate dwelling without allowing any failure of filial duty, and leaves the verb open.
Clarke derives the verb from bending down, body or mind, and declines to guess the subject; Wesley makes the field and the evening the fit place and time for such exercises.
Henry turns the scene into a discourse on solitude and on providences that find us in the way of our duty.

debates.question: What was Isaac doing in the field?

sides.position: meditating — the related noun is used of religious meditation, and it suits his character
praying, as the Targums render it, and probably for the success of this very errand
holders: Onkelos and Jonathan (as reported by Gill)

sides.position: either; the Hebrew allows both, and the Lord granted a token of his presence regardless

themes: alone in the field at evening
62.pericope_label: Isaac in the field at eventide

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the dismounting as eastern courtesy, sets this moment in the sequence of qualities the chapter has shown in her, and describes the bridal veil as far larger than the everyday one.

Calvin refutes the reading that she fell in fright, shows the question came before the dismounting, and derives the Latin word for marrying from the custom of veiling brides; Gill notes she asked as soon as she saw a man walking toward them.

Clarke observes that the word for the veil occurs here first and is of doubtful meaning, most taking it as the eastern sign of chastity and subjection; Wesley reads both gestures as humility, modesty and subjection.
Henry admires what she did not complain of, and applies the veil to those espoused to Christ.

debates.question: Why did Rebekah alight from the camel?

sides.position: in courtesy, as an inferior dismounts to meet a superior
struck with fear at the sight of him

outliers.note: Turns from the ancient custom to his own age, whose bridal apparel seems contrived for the subversion of all modesty.

schools.summary: Gill lists what the servant's report to Isaac must have contained, the chapter going over the same events a fourth time.

Henry dates the comfort three years after Sarah's death, reads the son's affection across into the husband's, and takes the chapter's very length as the lesson — providence is to be noticed in the little common occurrences of life.
Ellicott had appealed to this verse earlier as evidence that a wife of standing kept a tent of her own.

outliers.note: Holds that Scripture dwells on minute domestic circumstances and despatches great mysteries briefly on purpose, since it was not written for philosophers and statesmen only.

themes: the story told a fourth time
66.pericope_label: Isaac takes Rebekah, and is comforted
